items.q: A hash-map lookup in a Python dict costs, on average…
items.explain: Average-case constant time; worst case O(n) on pathological collisions — the caveat the interview wants you to mention.

items.q: Two pointers at opposite ends of a sorted array is the classic setup for…
items.explain: Opposite-end pointers solve pair-sum on sorted input in one linear pass — the pattern to name before coding.

items.q: BFS vs DFS on a graph: BFS is the natural choice when you need…
choices: The shortest path in an unweighted graph
items.explain: BFS expands level by level, so the first time it reaches a node is via the fewest edges.

items.q: In dynamic programming, memoization differs from tabulation in that it…
choices: Caches recursive results top-down instead of filling a table bottom-up
items.explain: Same recurrence, two directions: memoization caches top-down recursion; tabulation fills the table bottom-up.

items.q: A back-of-envelope estimate for a design interview should start with…
choices: Users, requests per second, reads vs writes, and storage
items.explain: Estimation grounds the design: QPS, read/write ratio, and storage growth decide which boxes you need.

items.q: The CAP theorem says a distributed store under partition must trade off between…
items.explain: When the network partitions, you choose: stay consistent (reject writes) or stay available (accept divergence).

items.q: An API endpoint that charges a credit card must be…
items.explain: Network retries are inevitable; idempotency keys make a retried charge a no-op instead of a double charge.

items.q: A composite index on (user_id, created_at) best serves…
choices: Queries filtering by user_id, optionally ordered by created_at
items.explain: Leftmost-prefix rule: the index serves user_id lookups and user_id + created_at ordering, not created_at alone.

items.q: READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ differs in…
choices: Whether a re-read inside one transaction can see newly committed rows
items.explain: REPEATABLE READ gives the transaction a stable snapshot; READ COMMITTED can see new commits on re-read (non-repeatable reads).

items.q: A cache stampede (thundering herd) happens when…
choices: Many requests miss simultaneously on an expired hot key and flood the database
items.explain: One expired popular key means N concurrent recomputes. Mitigate with request coalescing, jittered TTLs, or probabilistic early refresh.

items.q: At-least-once queue delivery requires consumers to be…
items.explain: Duplicates are possible by design; the consumer must handle redelivery without double-applying effects.

items.q: A saga replaces a distributed transaction with…
choices: A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure
items.explain: No distributed lock: each service commits locally, and failures trigger compensating transactions that undo prior steps.

items.q: setTimeout(..., 0) vs Promise.resolve().then(): the promise callback runs…
choices: Before the timeout: microtasks drain first
items.explain: Microtasks (promise callbacks) run before the next macrotask (setTimeout) — the event-loop ordering interviewers check first.

items.q: A stale closure in a React effect usually means…
choices: The effect captured an old state value because a dependency was missing
items.explain: Missing dependencies freeze captured values; the fix is declaring dependencies honestly or using refs and functional updates.

items.q: Keys in a React list exist so reconciliation can…
choices: Match elements across renders and preserve state
items.explain: Keys identify which element is which across renders; index keys break that identity on reorder and corrupt state.

items.q: Layout thrashing is caused by…
choices: Interleaved reads and writes of layout properties forcing repeated reflows
items.explain: Read-write-read-write on geometry forces the browser to reflow between each pair; batch reads, then batch writes.

items.q: CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures…
items.explain: CLS scores how much content jumps around; reserve space for images and ads, and avoid injecting content above existing content.

items.q: Debounce is preferred over throttle for a search typeahead because it…
choices: Waits for a pause in typing before firing one request
items.explain: Debounce fires after typing pauses — one request per thought instead of one per keystroke; throttle fires on a fixed cadence regardless.

items.q: SSR vs SSG: SSR renders…
choices: At build time for all pages
Per request on the server; SSG pre-renders at build time
items.explain: SSR = HTML per request (fresh data, slower TTFB); SSG = HTML at build (fast, stale until rebuilt); ISR splits the difference.

items.q: Storing a JWT in localStorage is risky because…
choices: Any XSS script can read it; httpOnly cookies are the safer default
items.explain: localStorage is JS-readable, so XSS exfiltrates the token. httpOnly cookies keep it out of JS reach (with CSRF mitigations).

items.q: The authorization-code OAuth flow keeps the client secret…
choices: On the backend: the browser never sees it
items.explain: The code is exchanged for tokens server-to-server; the secret never touches the browser — that is the flow's whole security point.

items.q: Validating on both client and server matters because…
choices: Client validation is UX; server validation is security — clients cannot be trusted
items.explain: Client validation improves UX but is bypassable; the server is the trust boundary and must re-validate everything.

items.q: A BFF (backend-for-frontend) exists to…
choices: Shape APIs per client (web vs mobile) instead of one generic API
items.explain: Each client gets an API shaped to its screens and constraints, avoiding over/under-fetching from a one-size API.

items.q: Blue-green deployment enables safe releases by…
choices: Running old and new versions side by side and switching traffic with instant rollback
items.explain: Two identical environments; traffic flips to green only when healthy, and flips back instantly on trouble.

items.q: A retain cycle in Swift most commonly comes from…
choices: Two objects holding strong references to each other, often via closures
items.explain: Strong reference cycles (object ↔ closure capturing self strongly) leak; break them with weak or unowned captures.

items.q: In SwiftUI, @StateObject vs @ObservedObject: @StateObject…
choices: Owns the object's lifetime; @ObservedObject borrows an externally owned one
items.explain: StateObject creates and owns the observable; ObservedObject references one owned elsewhere. Creating with ObservedObject causes recreation bugs.

items.q: UIKit work must happen on the main thread because…
choices: UIKit is not thread-safe; UI updates off-main cause undefined behavior
items.explain: UIKit classes are main-thread-only by contract; background completions must dispatch UI updates back to the main queue or actor.

items.q: A Swift actor prevents data races by…
choices: Serializing access to its isolated state
items.explain: Actors isolate mutable state and serialize access across suspension points — the compiler enforces what locks used to do by convention.

items.q: Storing an auth token belongs in…
items.explain: Keychain is the encrypted, access-controlled store for secrets; UserDefaults is not a safe home for credentials.

items.q: Core Data faults are…
choices: Lazily realized objects: placeholders that fire (load) on access
items.explain: Faulting keeps memory low by materializing objects only when touched — efficient, but firing faults on the wrong thread or context is a classic bug.

items.q: The !! operator in Kotlin…
choices: Asserts non-null and throws if wrong — the thing interviews want you to avoid
items.explain: !! converts a nullable to non-null by assertion; a wrong assertion crashes. Prefer safe calls, Elvis, or let.

items.q: A sealed class is preferred over an enum when…
choices: Variants must carry different data or state
items.explain: Sealed hierarchies let each subtype carry its own data (Success(data) vs Error(e)) while staying exhaustively matchable in when.

items.q: viewModelScope exists so coroutines…
choices: Are cancelled automatically when the ViewModel is cleared
Run on the main thread only
items.explain: Structured concurrency tied to the ViewModel lifecycle: no leaks across rotation or navigation, cancellation for free.

items.q: StateFlow vs SharedFlow: StateFlow…
choices: Holds the latest value and replays it to new collectors; SharedFlow is the configurable event bus
items.explain: StateFlow = observable state with a current value; SharedFlow = configurable hot events. Mixing them up is the classic interview trap.

items.q: Room migrations are required when…
choices: The schema version changes and old installs must upgrade without losing data
items.explain: Schema changes need explicit Migration objects mapping old to new; without them Room either crashes or destructively migrates user data away.

items.q: Doze mode affects background work by…
choices: Deferring alarms, jobs, and network to maintenance windows to save battery
items.explain: Doze batches background work into windows; WorkManager with the right constraints is the correct API, not foreground-style polling.

items.q: Declaring a hardware register pointer volatile tells the compiler…
choices: Not to cache or reorder accesses: every read and write hits the hardware
items.explain: volatile forbids optimizing away or reordering accesses — essential for memory-mapped registers that change outside program flow.

items.q: Priority inversion happens when…
choices: A low-priority task holds a lock a high-priority task needs, while a medium task preempts the low one
items.explain: The classic: medium-priority work starves the lock holder, delaying the high-priority task unboundedly. Priority inheritance is the standard fix.

items.q: An ISR should be short and non-blocking because…
choices: It runs with interrupts masked; long ISRs blow latency budgets and can deadlock on locks
items.explain: ISRs defer work to tasks via queues or semaphores; doing real work in the ISR destroys real-time guarantees.

items.q: DMA is valuable because it…
choices: Moves data between peripheral and memory without CPU involvement, freeing the core
items.explain: The DMA controller handles the transfer; the CPU gets an interrupt on completion instead of babysitting every byte.

items.q: Reading an unaligned multi-byte value on Cortex-M0 can…
choices: Fault: the M0 lacks hardware support for unaligned access
items.explain: Cortex-M0/M0+ fault on unaligned accesses (unlike M3/M4); packed structs and wire protocols must handle alignment explicitly.

items.q: A HardFault on Cortex-M is debugged first by…
choices: Reading the stacked registers (PC, LR, fault status) to find the faulting instruction and cause
items.explain: The exception frame holds PC/LR and the fault status registers name the cause — evidence before guesses.

items.q: The test pyramid argues for…
choices: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest e2e tests
items.explain: Cost and speed grow up the pyramid; the bulk of coverage belongs at the cheap, fast unit layer.

items.q: A mock differs from a stub in that a mock…
choices: Verifies interactions (was it called, with what); a stub just returns canned data
items.explain: Stubs provide indirect inputs; mocks assert on the interactions themselves — behavior verification vs state verification.

items.q: Playwright's auto-waiting means…
choices: Actions wait for actionability (visible, stable, enabled) before executing, cutting flake
items.explain: Auto-waiting retries until the element is actionable — the main reason Playwright suites flake less than raw WebDriver scripts.

items.q: p99 latency matters more than the mean because…
choices: The mean hides the slow tail users actually feel; p99 bounds the worst typical experience
items.explain: Averages wash out outliers; p99 says ‘99% of requests beat this’ — the SLA-relevant number.

items.q: A flaky test should first be…
choices: Quarantined and root-caused: timing, shared state, or order dependence
items.explain: Reruns mask the cause; quarantine stops the bleeding while you fix the timing, shared-state, or order bug — then it returns.

items.q: Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact-style) primarily protects against…
choices: Breaking API changes: the provider verifies it still satisfies each consumer's recorded expectations
items.explain: Consumers record their expectations; the provider replays them in CI, catching breaking changes before deployment.
